### To the pious prince Josaphat, who abandoned all things for the sake of Christ, by Jacques de Billy, Abbot of Saint-Michel-en-l'Herm, brother of the venerable Father in Christ Jean de Billy, Prior of the Carthusian monastery of Bonne-Espérance. <note>original Latin: "Ad pium principem Iosaphat... *When delights were a torment to you, and scepters but chains,*
*When riches were as dust, and dishonor was your honor:*
*What can I say, but that you were steeped in the new wine of the spirit, drinking*
*That which makes a man at once forgetful of himself?*
*For to prefer a sackcloth to a kingdom, and the world’s hardships*
*To its sweetness—what creates this, if not a holy intoxication?*
*Glowing with this wine, you were worthy of such a translator:*

*Has left everything behind to follow after true riches.*

### SONNET BY THE SAME AUTHOR, to the Reader.

Do you desire to quickly acquire
Lands and goods? (says a son of lies),
Read Galen, <note>Galen of Pergamum (c. 129–216 AD) was the most famous physician of the Roman Empire. The author is suggesting that if you want worldly wealth, you should study lucrative professions like medicine or law.</note> or plunge into those books
Which do nothing but discuss lawsuits.
Do you desire to make yourself poor here below,
To be rich in heaven in truth, and not in a dream,
And for goods that the moth cannot gnaw,
Nor the length of time cause to rot?
Take this book from me, and with a diligent hand
Often present it before your eyes.
Do you wish to know what benefit will come to you?
For your contempt of transitory greatness,
You shall have the wealth and glory of heaven;
That is the fruit your soul will take from it.

# NOTICE
->to the Reader.<-

My dear Reader, I wish to inform you that the present History is included within the Works of Saint John Damascene <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD) was a prominent Christian monk and scholar. While this story was long attributed to him, it is actually a Christianized version of the life of the Buddha.</note>, and is attributed to him by many; this is what moved me to publish it under his name. Nevertheless, an old Greek manuscript was shared with me by Monsieur de Saint-André (a very learned man and a lover of all fine literature) in which I found a Preface to our History under the name of a good hermit of Mount Sinai named John, a person of great holiness and endowed with the gift of prophecy, who flourished in the time of the Emperor Theodore, the first of that name <note>Theodore I Laskaris (reigned 1204–1222). The "John" mentioned may be an attempt to link the text to John Climacus, a famous Sinai monk, though the chronologies do not perfectly align.</note>. I have seen fit to join this to our translation, leaving everyone the freedom to judge which of the two is the Author. Regardless, both are very ancient and persons of great authority. Know likewise that in the Latin copy there are almost as many errors as words, and had it not been that my brother, the Lord Abbot of Saint-Michel-en-l'Herm <note>Jacques de Billy (1535–1581), a renowned Greek scholar and theologian.</note>—a man very well-versed in Greek and Latin letters (as can be seen by the translation he made of Saint Gregory Nazianzus)—took the trouble to compare it with the handwritten Greek manuscript and correct the heavy errors he found there, I would have been left stranded along the way, finding neither rhyme nor reason in the ancient version. If you find anything here that satisfies your spirit, in return, pray to God for the two brothers.

<summary>In this preface, Jean de Billy explains the conflicting attributions of the text (John Damascene vs. John of Sinai) and credits his brother, Jacques de Billy, for correcting the flawed Latin version against a Greek manuscript.</summary>

# NARRATION
## of the History.

INDIA is a very large and well-populated region, located very far from the land of Egypt; on the side of that land, the Sea surrounds it on all sides, and on the side of the mainland, it borders the land of Persia. The said land was once deeply obscured by the shadows of idolatry <note>The author uses "idolatry" here to describe the pre-Christian religions of the East, setting the stage for a conversion narrative.</note>, and the people were barbaric and inhuman, and given to all vices, when the only Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, not being able to bear seeing his creature <note>original: "sa creature" — meaning mankind as God's creation.</note> oppressed by the servitude of sin, moved by mercy, appeared in a likeness to us, except for sin: and not at all abandoning the throne of the Father, took up residence in the body of the Virgin for our salvation, so that our dwelling may be in the heavens, and that we might be raised from the ancient fall, and that, delivered from sin, we might recover our initial adoption as children <note>original: "adoption filiale" — referring to the theological concept of humans being adopted into God's family through Christ.</note>.

Then Josaphat said to him: O man, you tell me of great things, magnificent and admirable, and worthy of fear and trembling—if it is indeed as you say, and that after death and the dissolution of the body, there is <term>resurrection</term> <note>The rising from the dead at the end of time, a central tenet of the faith Barlaam is teaching.</note> and <term>regeneration</term> <note>The spiritual rebirth or the renewal of the world.</note>, and joy and gladness, and glory for the good, and for the wicked, pain and torment. <meta>This page continues Barlaam’s explanation of the mechanics of human choice. Having previously defined free will as the movement of the rational soul, he now breaks down the logical steps—consultation, judgment, and "sentence"—that lead to an "election" or final choice.</meta>

# HISTORY OF BARLAAM

[...consultation as to whether] one ought to do a thing or not, and afterwards one judges what is most expedient; and this is called judgment. Afterward, one sets their affection upon what was found through consultation, and this is called sentence <note>In this context, "sentence" refers to a settled mental decision or an internal resolve, rather than a legal verdict.</note>. For if one judges it, but does not take an affection to what has been judged—that is to say, if one does not love it and acquiesce to it—that is not called a sentence. And after the affection, the choice and election are made. For election is nothing other than choosing one of two proposed things and leaving the other. And it is quite manifest that consultation is an election made with judgment, even by the etymology of the word: for a thing elected <note>original: "eſleüe"</note> is as much as to say chosen above another. Now, no one judges or settles upon a matter before having deliberated; nor likewise does one choose, until first having judged and settled that it is expedient; for we do not set ourselves to carry out every thing that seems good and expedient to us. Then, and not before, that which was judged through consultation becomes an election, when the appetite and the will concur in it. And from this it is gathered that election is a desire for things within our power, having passed through counsel. For that which was previously judged with counsel, we desire thereafter by choosing it: considering that all counsel is taken for that which is to be done; and thus before every choice, counsel precedes, and before every action, election marches forward. And therefore not only the actions, but also

<margin>Of what use are the Relics of the Saints.</margin>

<margin>By the touching of the Relics we acquire sanctification.</margin>

And the King said once more: "If the memory of death is profitable (as you say), why do you not take that memory from the bones of your own bodies—which are truly yours and which will shortly turn to rot—rather than taking it from these foreign bodies, already corrupted and decayed?"

Then the Monk replied: "Since I have told you five causes and reasons for which we carry the Relics of the saints with us, and you respond to only one, it seems that you are mocking us."

<term>Barlaam</term>: The hermit who converted Josaphat.

<term>Memory of death</term>: *Memento mori*; a spiritual practice of reflecting on mortality to remain humble and focused on the afterlife.
<term>Sanctification</term>: The process of being made holy or purified through divine grace.
<term>Monk</term>: A member of a religious community living under vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience.

trampled upon by them; it is not one and the same nature, but rather they are divided wills, and all of them malicious: and therefore none of them is God.

**IT IS** therefore, Sire, a manifest thing that the entire physiology <note>In this context, "physiology" refers to the study of the nature, origins, and physical existence of the gods.</note> of the gods is an error. But how is it that the Philosophers and learned Greeks have not understood that the authors of laws are judged by their own laws? For if the laws are just, certainly their gods are unjust, having committed wicked acts—that is to say, among themselves, homicides, and poisonings, and adulteries, and thefts, and sodomies. But if they have done well, to tell the truth, then the laws are unjust, being made against the gods. Now, it is certain that the laws are just and good, praising good things and forbidding the doing of evil things; and the works of these gods are iniquitous, and all those who consider them gods are wicked and worthy of death. For if their histories are fabulous <note>meaning "composed of fables" or fictional stories</note>, they are but words; if they are physical <note>This refers to "euhemerism" or "naturalism," the theory that gods were originally just natural forces or deceased humans.</note>, then those who performed and suffered these things are not gods; and if these histories are written allegorically, they are fables and nothing else. Therefore, Sire, I have clearly proven that all these manners of worshipping so many gods are works of error and perdition: for it is not fitting to call "gods" visible things which do not see; rather, it is necessary that all worship the invisible God, who sees all things, and who is the creator of everything.

# THE LIFE OF ST. JOHN DAMAS-
*cene, composed long ago by John, Patriarch of Jerusalem, shortened and put into English by the Translator of the present History, with a Homily by Saint John Chrysostom.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a figure (possibly a saint or angel) amidst ornate foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

<margin>Damascus, the capital city of Syria.</margin>
Saint John, born in Damascus, the capital city of Syria—from which he even takes his name—and once honored by the conversion of Saint Paul, had as his father a man of great authority. This man was established as the superintendent of the affairs of the people, as much for the integrity of his character as because he was rich and powerful in wealth. These riches, certainly, he did not squander lavishly on delights, drunkenness, and <term>vain display: the original French "bobans" refers to ostentatious or extravagant show</term>, but rather he employed all that he could gather for the ransom of Christian prisoners. And of all his lands and lordships that he possessed, both in Judea and in Palestine, he reserved for himself only what was necessary for him to pass through this life. And such was the virtue and humanity of this personage that, though possessing great wealth, he <note>original: "en iouyssoit comme n'en iouyssant point"; an allusion to 1 Corinthians 7:31, suggesting a detachment from worldly goods.</note> enjoyed it as if he enjoyed it not, being more careful to seek the things that concern the salvation of the soul. While he was thus occupied in such good and laudable practices, a son was born to him, whom he had baptized and named John:

Added to this is that the enjoyment of Empire and preeminence ends with this life, or to speak more truly, abandons its lovers even while they are still living: it has even rendered many extremely miserable, plunging them into the deep abyss of shame and confusion.

<margin>The solitary life brings great rewards in this world and the next.</margin>
But the life led in solitude—beyond the fact that in this world it fills the righteous with all good things—will also lead them, joyful and vigorous, before the tribunal of God our Savior upon their departure from here; at which time most Kings and great Princes will receive very heavy punishment for their sins and misdeeds.

**LET US COMPARE** therefore the rewards of the Monastic life to those which have only the appearance of goodness—such as those which come from the power and glory of this world—and let us contemplate the difference between these two types of goods: for the comparison of the two will give us a clearer understanding—

Even when comparing together that which holds the supreme degree of honor and worldly good—which is Empire and kingship—to the life of Religion and solitude, let us consider the fruit that each brings. The Empire of the Prince, then, is to command a great number of cities, regions, and peoples: to create Magistrates, Captains, and Senators; to raise troops, set up camps, and dispose of the affairs of his Empire as it seems good to him. But he who has dedicated himself entirely to God and has embraced the solitary life, holds under his power anger, envy, avarice, pleasure—in short, <margin>*What is the continual care of a Monk*</margin> everything that is repugnant to virtue. He is always careful to prevent his spirit from being overcome by vices, and to keep reason from becoming subject to sensuality; helping himself with the fear <margin>*To what the fear of God is useful.*</margin> of God to tame every evil and vicious affection, and to direct his understanding toward the contemplation of heavenly things.

## OF THE COMPARISON

...God, and armed with celestial and divine weapons, does not carry away the honor and the prize. And as for the King, you will find him fighting the Barbarians, who certainly are not nearly as furious, nor as terrible, nor as powerful as devils; and therefore, even if he were to overcome them, the victory of the Monk is far more distinguished, having dealt with a much stronger and more powerful enemy. For if you wish to inquire into the causes for which each one enters into combat, you will judge them to be very different. For the Monk <note>original: *Religieux*</note> wages continual war against the devil, to maintain piety within himself and to persevere in the service of God; or to pull towns and villages out of the abyss of error and to announce to them the word of salvation. As for the King, he wars against Barbarians to guard the cities, provinces, and treasures he has seized by force; or to conquer anew some country or region, driven by ambition and damnable avarice. And it has often happened to many Princes that, while trying to aggrandize themselves and extend and amplify their borders, they have been dispossessed and chased from the lands they previously enjoyed.

### OF THE KING AND OF THE MONK.
Aa ij

<margin>*Cruelty of the men of war.*</margin>
...[even when he wins, he allows] his soldiers to ravish, plunder, and rob passers-by; to besiege towns and pillage the houses of good people, demanding from their hosts what no law permits, under the pretext of I know not what ancient custom—one that is unjust and contrary to the law. Yet, in all these evils, the Prince burdens only the poor, not the rich; as if he truly feared those who are wealthy.

But it is not so with the Monk. For when he appears in public, he brings some gift with which he favors both the rich and the poor. He is dressed in a single, very simple robe, drinking water more willingly than wine, no matter how good or noble <note>original: *genereux*; in the context of wine, this means a high-quality, potent, or "noble" vintage</note> the wine may be. He asks nothing from the rich for himself, but instead often petitions and asks on behalf of those in need, bringing profit both to the one who gives and the one who receives. Thus, he becomes a common physician to both the rich and the poor, delivering the rich from sin through holy admonition <note>original: *faincte admonitiõ*; the act of giving spiritual advice or a mild rebuke to steer someone away from sin</note>, and relieving the poverty of the indigent.

As for the King, if he reduces the taxes <term>tailles: a direct land tax in pre-revolutionary France that fell mostly on the peasantry</term> and salt-taxes <term>gabelles: a notoriously unpopular and regressive tax on salt</term>, he provides more benefit to the rich than to the poor. But if he increases them, then those who lack great wealth are most grievously oppressed. For the levying of taxes and collection of funds, however great they may be, can do only little harm to the rich; meanwhile, like a rushing torrent, they sweep away the entire households of the poor, and fill...

<note>This section, often called an "Errata," was a common feature in early printed books where the printer listed mistakes discovered after the pages had already been set in type.</note>

Folio 122, page 2, line 4. "coient" for "believe" <note>original: "croient"</note>.
Folio 166, page 2, line 15. "l'eprit," read "the spirit" <note>original: "l'esprit"</note>.

--- Page 423 ---
<meta>This page follows the conclusion of the Table of Contents and the errata list. It provides the legal authorization for the book's publication, known as the "Privilège du Roi" (Royal Privilege), which served as an early form of copyright protection in 16th-century France.</meta>

# EXTRACT OF THE
# ROYAL PRIVILEGE.

By the grace and privilege of the King, permission is granted to Guillaume Chaudiere, Merchant Bookseller at the University of Paris, to print or have printed, one or several times, a book entitled, *History of Barlaam and Josaphat King of the Indies, etc. Composed by Saint John Damascene. And translated into English <note>original: "François" — following the convention of making the text accessible to the modern reader while noting the original source language.</note> by F. Jean de Billy, Prior of the Charterhouse <term>Charterhouse: A monastery of the Carthusian order, known for their silence and solitude.</term> of Our Lady of Good Hope near Gaillon.* And the said Lord <note>The "Lord" here refers to King Henry III of France.</note> forbids all others of our Kingdom, of whatever quality they may be, from printing or having printed, selling, or distributing in his lands, territories, and Seigniories the said book, without the leave and consent of the said Chaudiere, until the time and term of nine entire and consecutive years after the first printing that shall be made of the said book, upon the penalties contained in the Letters Patent <term>Letters Patent: An open document issued by a monarch to grant a right, monopoly, or title.</term> of the said Lord. And we will that to the Vidimus <term>Vidimus: From the Latin "we have seen," this is an official copy of a legal document, certified to be as valid as the original.</term> of these made under the Royal seal, faith be added as if to the original. Given at Paris, the twelfth day of September, the year of grace one thousand five hundred seventy-four, and of our reign the first.

->By the Council.<-

->Signed DANES.<-

<summary>This page contains the official royal license granting Guillaume Chaudiere the exclusive rights to publish Jean de Billy's translation of the "History of Barlaam and Josaphat" for nine years. Issued in 1574, it highlights the legal protections and monastic origins of the translation during the first year of Henry III's reign.</summary>
<keywords>Royal Privilege, copyright, Guillaume Chaudiere, Jean de Billy, Saint John Damascene, Barlaam and Josaphat, 16th-century printing, Henry III of France, Charterhouse of Gaillon</keywords>
